group.title: Food and eating out
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: The particular taste of a food or drink.
examples: This ice cream comes in three {flavors}.
wrong: The soup has a strong flavor, so it tastes of nothing.

words.meaning: Salty or spicy, not sweet.
examples: I prefer {savory} snacks like chips to candy.
wrong: Chocolate cake is my favorite savory dish.

words.meaning: Containing a lot of sugar.
examples: Try not to drink too many {sugary} drinks.
wrong: This sugary cereal has no sugar in it at all.

words.meaning: Hard and dry in a nice way, so it breaks easily when you bite it.
examples: I love {crispy} fried chicken.
wrong: The crispy toast was soft and wet.

words.meaning: Full of juice and pleasant to eat.
examples: These oranges are sweet and {juicy}.
wrong: The juicy peach was dry and hard as wood.

words.meaning: To cook meat or vegetables in an oven or over a fire.
examples: We {roasted} a chicken for Sunday lunch.
wrong: She roasted the vegetables by putting them in the freezer.

words.meaning: To cook food over or under strong direct heat.
examples: Dad {grilled} burgers in the backyard.
wrong: He grilled the fish by keeping it in cold water.

words.meaning: To cut food into small pieces with a knife.
examples: {Chop} the onions into small pieces.
wrong: She chopped the carrots by leaving them whole.

words.meaning: To take the skin off fruit or vegetables.
examples: {Peel} the potatoes before you boil them.
wrong: I peeled the banana and ate the skin.

words.meaning: To move a spoon around in a liquid to mix it.
examples: {Stir} the sauce so it doesn’t burn.
wrong: He stirred his coffee by leaving the spoon on the table.

words.meaning: To rub food against a tool with small holes to cut it into thin strips.
examples: {Grate} some cheese over the pasta.
wrong: She grated the cheese into one big block.

words.meaning: An amount of food for one person.
examples: The {portions} at this restaurant are huge.
wrong: A portion is the whole pot of food for everyone.

words.meaning: A small dish eaten before the main part of a meal.
examples: We shared some soup as an {appetizer}.
wrong: We ordered an appetizer to finish the meal after dessert.

words.meaning: The biggest and most important dish of a meal.
examples: For the {main course} I had steak and fries.
wrong: The main course is the small sweet dish at the end of the meal.

words.meaning: A small amount of food served with the main dish.
examples: The steak comes with a {side dish} of salad.
wrong: A side dish is the biggest plate of the meal.

words.meaning: Looking or smelling so good that you want to eat it.
examples: The bakery is full of {mouthwatering} cakes.
wrong: The mouthwatering food looked so bad that nobody wanted to try it.

words.meaning: A skilled cook, especially the main cook in a restaurant.
examples: The {chef} cooks all the meals himself.
wrong: The chef works in the restaurant but never goes into the kitchen.

words.meaning: To arrange in advance to eat at a restaurant at a certain time.
examples: I’ll call the restaurant to {book a table} for eight o’clock.
wrong: We booked a table, so we just turned up without calling.

words.meaning: Cooked food you buy at a restaurant to eat somewhere else.
examples: Let’s get Chinese {takeout} tonight.
wrong: We had takeout, so we sat in the restaurant to eat it.

words.meaning: A person who does not eat or use anything that comes from animals.
examples: As a {vegan}, she doesn’t drink milk or eat eggs.
wrong: He’s a vegan, so he eats steak and cheese every day.

words.meaning: Milk and foods made from milk, such as cheese and yogurt.
examples: I can’t eat {dairy}, so no cheese for me.
wrong: Dairy foods like bread and rice are made from milk.

words.meaning: Fish and shellfish from the sea that people eat.
examples: This town is famous for its fresh {seafood}.
wrong: Chicken and beef are my favorite kinds of seafood.

words.meaning: Birds such as chickens and ducks kept for meat and eggs, or their meat.
examples: The shop sells meat, {poultry} and fish.
wrong: Poultry is meat that comes from pigs and cows.

words.meaning: Food that is not eaten during a meal and is kept for later.
examples: We had the {leftovers} from dinner for lunch the next day.
wrong: There were no leftovers, so we put the rest in the fridge.

words.meaning: Made at home, not bought in a shop.
examples: Nothing beats {homemade} bread.
wrong: This homemade jam was made in a big factory.

words.meaning: Having a good, strong flavor.
examples: The soup was hot and {tasty}.
wrong: The meal was so tasty that nobody wanted to eat it.

words.meaning: The feeling that you want to eat food.
examples: Swimming always gives me a big {appetite}.
wrong: She had a huge appetite, so she didn’t want to eat.

words.meaning: Very hungry.
examples: I’m {starving}, let’s eat now.
wrong: I’m starving, so I’ll skip lunch.

words.meaning: To drop small amounts of something over a surface.
examples: {Sprinkle} some sugar on top of the cake.
wrong: She sprinkled the salt by pouring the whole bag into one spot.

words.meaning: A meal where you serve yourself from many dishes on a table.
examples: The hotel breakfast is a {buffet}.
wrong: At the buffet, a waiter brings each dish to your table.

words.meaning: A piece of cloth or paper for wiping your mouth and hands at a meal.
examples: He wiped his mouth with a {napkin}.
wrong: She ate her soup with a napkin instead of a spoon.

words.meaning: Kept very cold so that it becomes hard and stays fresh.
examples: We bought some {frozen} peas.
wrong: The frozen pizza was warm and soft when it came out of the freezer.

words.meaning: No longer fresh, and often hard and dry.
examples: The bread was {stale}, so we fed it to the birds.
wrong: This stale bread was baked five minutes ago.

words.meaning: Gone bad and soft so it cannot be eaten.
examples: Throw away the {rotten} apples.
wrong: These rotten eggs are fresh and perfect to eat.

words.meaning: Cooked for too long.
examples: The pasta was {overcooked} and soft.
wrong: The meat was overcooked, so it was still raw inside.

words.meaning: Of meat, cooked all the way through.
examples: I like my steak {well-done}, with no pink inside.
wrong: His well-done steak was red and raw in the middle.

words.meaning: To have a meal in a restaurant rather than at home.
examples: We {eat out} every Friday night.
wrong: We ate out by cooking dinner in our own kitchen.

words.meaning: A polite way of telling a guest to take some food or drink freely.
examples: There’s plenty of cake, so please {help yourself}.
wrong: Help yourself to the cake, but don’t take any.

words.meaning: Covered in or full of oil or fat.
examples: The fries were too {greasy} for me.
wrong: The greasy food had no oil or fat in it at all.

words.meaning: Of meat, soft and easy to cut and chew.
examples: The beef was so {tender} it melted in my mouth.
wrong: The tender steak was so tough that I couldn’t cut it.
